newsitem.title: USA: U.S. industry girds for new air quality proposal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. industry girds for new air quality proposal.

text.p: Industry groups and health advocates are readying for battle as the Environmental Protection Agency prepares this week to unveil tighter air quality standards.
The proposal to set stricter levels for smog and fine particles is expected to be announced around Nov. 29.
"The politics of this is about to get even hotter over the next several days," said Paul Bailey, health and environmental affairs director of the American Petroleum Institute.

Most industry and environmental groups are expecting the the EPA to call for a stricter ozone or smog standard of about 0.08 parts per million, compared with the current standard that allows a concentration of 0.12 parts per million measured over a one-hour period.

The agency is also expected to propose standards on particles as small as 2.5 microns in diameter, allowing concentrations of up to 65 micrograms per cubic meter. Under current rules, the EPA focuses on slightly larger particles, 10 microns in diameter, allowing concentrations up to 150 micrograms per cubic meter in one day.

Utilities and manufacturers fear the tighter standards could result in heavier, costly controls on their plants, and oil companies see the tighter standards resulting in more counties being required to use cleaner-burning gasoline.
Health advocates say the tighter standards would prolong tens of thousands of lives.
"We have a serious health concern on our hands," said Deborah Shprentz of the Natural Resources Defense Council.
While agreeing that air pollution harmed health, Bailey said: "At issue is which air pollutants cause the health effects and at what level."

Industry groups said there are too few monitors measuring for particles as small as 2.5 microns, therefore it was too early to say whether limiting those particles would significantly improve people's health.
Environmental and industry groups last week met with EPA Administrator Carol Browner and separately with White House officials who are reviewing EPA's proposals.
One industry lobbyist who attended the meetings said EPA tried to reassure small businesses that they would not be affected by the new standards.

"They said....we'll take care of you all in the implementation phase," the industry lobbyist said. But businesses are concerned that it will be up to states to decide how they will meet the new standards, so there was no way to predict what would happen once the standards were finalized next year.
EPA officials declined to comment on what they told the groups.

Environmentalists, while expecting a stronger standard, are uneasy that if it does not specify which pollutants should be controlled, states which are less environmentally-conscious might not go after the most dangerous pollutants, such as sulfur dioxide.
"There's a lot of wiggle room," said a clean air advocate.
The industry groups said they want the EPA's proposal to include the option of maintaining the current standards, instead of just proposing a new standard.
Bailey predicted that if the EPA came out with stronger standards, officials from cities, counties, states and industry would press for major changes in the Clean Air Act.
